 CRITICAL EVALUATIO~:

  Solubi11ty of Hydrogen Chloride in Solvents Containing Nitrogen.
  Solub1l1ty in nitrobenzene has been measured at barometric pressure over a
  temperature range by Zetkin et a1.(1) and by Ahmed et a1.(2). O'Brien (3)
  measured solubi11ties at various temperatures over a partial pressure range
  to 69.8 kPa. The evaluator has estimated solubilities at a part1al
  pressure of 101.3 kPa from O'Brien's measurements by assuming that the
  change in mole fraction solub1l1ty w1th partial pressure can be
  approx1mated by an equat10n of the the Krichevskii-Il'inskaya type. The
  evaluator has also estimated mole fract10n solubilities at a partial
  pressure of 101.3 kPa from mole fract10n solubilities of total pressures
  of approx1mately 101.3 kPa published by Zetkin et a1. and by Ahmed et a1.
  Mole fract10n solub1lities at a part1al pressure of 101.3 kPa 1n the
  range 253.15 K to 433.15 K from the three sources fit the equation:
        In x HCl   =    -39.613   +   3208.7/( T/K )     +    4.5790 In (T/K)

       Standard dev1ation in values of x HCl                 5.02 x 10- 3

  The solub1lity of hydrogen chloride in nitrobenzene in the presence of
  water for part1al pressures of gas up to 133.5 kPa at 298.15 K may be
  calculated from data pub11shed by Wynne-Jones (4). The mole fraction
  solubi11ty for a partial pressure of 101.3 kPa has been estimated from
  these data by the evaluator to be 0.070. The value for solub1l1ty in dry
  n1trobenzene from the equation given above is 0.063 ±0.005. The
  presence of water may therefore have l1ttle effect on the solub1lity of
  hydrogen chloride 1n nitrobenzene.
  Solubi11ty in chloronitrobenzenes and d1chloronitrobenzenes were measured
  by Zetk1n et a1.(1) over temperature ranges. Measurements indicate that
  substitut10n of chlorine 1nto the benzene nucleus reduces mole fraction
  solubility of hydrogen chloride as can be seen 1n the follow1ng table:
           Mole fraction solub1lities at P HCl         = 101.3 kPa
                                              333.15 K        373.15 K

           Nitrobenzene (1)                    0.0332          0.0196
           1-Chloro-2-nitrobenzene             0.0250          0.0150
           1-Chloro-3-nitrobenzene             0.0228          0.0140
           1-Chloro-4-nitrobenzene                             0.0175
           1,2-Dichloro-4-n1trobenzene         0.0206          0.0127
           1,3-D1chloro-2-nitrobenzene         0.0222          0.0112

  Data presented by Zetkin are self-consistent and may be accepted on a
  tentat1ve bas1s. No measurements by other workers on these chlorinated
  compounds are available for comparison.
  O'Brien et a1.(5) measured the solubility of hydrogen chloride over
  pressure ranges below barometric pressure in 1-methyl-2-nitrobenzene at
  298.15 K and in 1-methyl-3-nitrobenzene at 298.15 K and 308.15 K. Mole
  fraction solub1lities for partial pressures of 1.013 bar may be found by
  extrapolation of measurements at lower pressures. These are slightly
  h1gher than corresponding values for nitrobenzene itself as estimated from
  the smooth1ng equation given above.

 No other measurements on these methyln~trobenzenes are ava~lable for
 comparison but the data may be accepted on a tentative basis until further
 work is pUblished on the systems.
 Kosorotov et a1.(6) measured solub~lities ~n chlorinated methylpyridines
 under barometr~c pressure ~n the temperature range 333 K to 473 K. The
 follow~ng compounds were stud~ed:

        2-(trichloromethyl)pyr~d~ne             (A)
       2-chloro-6-(tr~chloromethyl)pyridine              (B)
        3,5-d~chloro-2-(tr~chloromethyl)pyr~d~ne (C)
        3,4,5-trichloro-2-(dichloromethyl)pyrid~ne(0)

 Solubil~ties were reported as molar concentrations except in the case of
 A at 378 K. In this case they reported the mole ratio composition of
 the "thIck pasty substance" wh~ch was formed. Solvents B, C & 0, show a
 linear variation of log (Solub~lIty/mol dm- 3 ) with 1/(T/K). Solvent A
 behaves ~n a similar manner above about 423 K. Between 378 K and 423 K
 there ~s a marked decrease in the molar concentrat~on and mole fraction of
 hydrogen chloride. The mole fraction of hydrogen chloride in the "pasty
 substance" at 378 K is 0.28.  The mole fractIons ~n the l~qu~d phase at
 393 K, 408 K and 423 K are about 0.24, 0.063, and 0.026, respectIvely.
 This decl~ne ~s consistent with decreas~ng stabil~ty of an ~on~c compound
 from the components.
 Molar concentrations of hydrogen chloride in the four solvents at the same
 temperature are in the order: A > C = 0 > B. This ~s not ~n order of
 increas~ng chlorine content.  Densit~es of B, C, and 0 are not available
 and mole fraction solubilities cannot be compared.
 There is no reason to doubt the rel~ability of the measurements which may
 be accepted on a tentative basis. Further measurements are requ~red for
 confirmation of the data.

 CRITICAL EVALUATION:
       The Solubility of Hydrogen Chloride     ~n   Solvents Containing Sulfur.
 The solubil~t~es of hydrogen chlor~de in a wide range of sulfur compounds have
 been measured by Gerrard and co-workers (1-3) at a total pressure equal to
 barometr~c pressure and at one or more temperatures.


 The mole fraction solubility in sulfuric ac~d at 273.15 K and 1.013 bar ~s low
 « 0.0196 ) but ~s apprec~ably higher ~n the butyl esters of sulfon~c ac~ds ~n
 which one of the hydroxyl groups in sulfur~c ac~d has been replaced by an alkyl
 or aryl group and the other hydroxyl group esterified. Solubil~ty ~s greater in
 alkyl sulfonic ac~ds than in benzenesulfon~c ac~d. Substitut~on of a methyl
 group ~nto the benzene nucleus of benzenesulfon~c ac~d ~ncreases the solub~lity.
 substitut~on of a chlorine atom lowers the solub~l~ty_


 Mole fraction solubilities are h~gh ~n sulfones in which both hydroxyl groups
 of sulfuric acid have been replaced by alkyl groups. Solub~l~ty is appreciably
 lower but st~ll above the reference l~ne value ~n benzene sulfuryl chlor~de ~n
 wh~ch one group has been replaced by the phenyl group and the other by chlor~ne.
 Solubil~ty falls below the reference l~ne in the case of sulfuryl chlor~de ~n
 which both hydroxyl groups have been replaced by chlor~ne.
 The available mole     fract~o~ solub~lity data    are   ~n   the order :
  sulfuric acid < sulfuryl chlor~de < benzene sulfonyl chlor~de <
  methanesulfonyl chloride < ethanesulfonyl chlor~de < chlorosulfon~c acid
  butyl ester < 2-propanesulfonyl chloride < 4-chlorobenzenesulfon~c acid,
  butyl ester < benzenesulfon~c acid, butyl ester < 4-methylbenzenesulfonic
  ac~d, butyl ester < methanesulfonic ac~d, butyl ester < ethanesulfon~c
  acid, butyl ester < tetrahydrothiophene-1 ,1-d~ox~de ( tetramethylene
  sulfone) < 1,1 '-sulfonylb~spropane ( d~propyl sulfone) <
  1,1 '-sulfonylbisbutane (dibutyl sulfone) < 2,2'-sulfonylbispropane
  (diisopropyl sulfone)

 There is a discrepancy between the mole fraction solubility in sulfuryl chloride
 at 273.15 K and a total pressure of 1.013 bar from Ahmed's (3) data (0.043), and
 that from Charalambous et B1.(2) (0.031). There is also a d~screpancy between
 data from these two sources for mole fraction solubility at 298.15 K and th~s
 total pressure in benzenesulfonyl chloride. The value from Charalambous et B1.
 is 0.0403 but the value from an extrapolation of Ahmed's data ~s 0.046.

 In general the data for sulfuric acid and its derivat~ves fall into a consistent
 overall pattern and there is no reason to doubt the reliab~lity of th~s pattern.
 Further work is needed to confirm the precise magnitude of solub~lit~es ~n this
 class of solvents.
 The solubility in thionyl chloride, at a total pressure equal to barometric, was
 measured by Ahmed in the temperature range 248.15 K to 273.15 K and by
 Domeniconi et B1.(4) at 298.15 K. Extrapolation of Ahmed's data ~nd~cates a
 mole fraction solubility of 0.0095 at 298.15 K. This is in sharp contrast to
 the value of 0.0195 from the data published by Domeniconi et B1. Further work
 on this system is required.
 The measurement of the solubility in liquid hydrogen sulfide by Quam & Wilkinson
 (5) must be considered to be semi-quantitative. The solubility ~n several
 solvents, in which one or both hydrogen atoms have been replaced by an alkyl or
 the phenyl group, have been measured by Frazer and Gerrard (1). Data for
 273.15 K and a total pressure of 101.3 kPa indicate that the mole fract~on
 solubilities in the compounds studied lie above the reference line value
 corresponding to Raoult's law and are in the order:
  benzenethiol < 1-butanethiol < 1,1 '-thiobisbenzene < 2-propanethiol <
  1,1 '-th~obisbutane < 1,1 '-thiobispropane.

CRITICAL EVALUATION:

Frazer & Gerrard (1) also reported solub1l1t1es 1n th10phene and
tetrahydrothiophene at 273.15 K and a total pressure equal to barometr1c.  In
line with the behaviour of other sulfur compounds, the solub1l1ty was markedly
greater in tetrahydrothiophene than in the unsaturated th1ophene.

The data for thiols, thioethers, thiophene and tetrahydroth10phene pub11shed by
Frazer & Gerrard are self cons1stent and l1kely to be reliable.  However further
measurements on these systems are needed for conf1rmat1on of data.

Solubilities at a total pressure equal to barometr1c pressure have been reported
by Ahmed (3) for d1ssolut1on in sulfur d10xide over the temperature range
218.15 K to 253.15 K and by Chesterman (6) for d1ssolut1on 1n carbon d1sulf1de
at 298.15 K.  Data for these two solvents require conf1rmat1on by other
workers.

 CRITICAL EVALUATION:

        Solub1lity of Hydrogen Chlor1de 1n Solvents Containing Boron.

 Solubilities 1n various boron compounds over temperature ranges at barometric
 pressure have been measured by Gerrard and his co-workers (1-3). The data are
 self-cons1stent and likely to be rel1able but there are no data by other workers
 for compar1son.

 Solub111ties in the triethyl, tr1butyl and tr1pentyl esters of boric acid were
 1nvest1gated over a temperature range of 199.15 K to 321.15 K. As with many
 solvents contain1ng oxygen, mole fract10n solubilit1es are higher than reference
 l1ne values corresponding to the Raoult's law equat10n i.e. ratio of partial
 pressure of hydrogen chlor1de to vapor pressure of l1qu1d hydrogen chloride at
 the same temperature.

 Mole fraction solubilit1es 1n d1oxaboroles are lower than 1n the non-cycl1c
 borates. The solub1l1ty 1ncreases w1th S1ze of the substituent alkoxy group.
 The presence of a benzene ring lowers the solub1l1ty. Mole fraction
 solub111t1es at 101.3 kPa and 293.15 K are as follows:
      (reference 11ne value                         0.024)
      2-butoxy-1,3,2-d10xaborolane                  0.123
      2-methoxy -1,3,2-benzod10xaborole             0.0853
      2-ethoxy-1,3,2-benzodioxaborole               0.109
      2-propoxy-1,3,2-benzod1oxaborole              0.115
      2-butoxy-1,3,2-benzod1oxaborole               0.118
      2-pentoxy-1,3,2-benzodioxaborole              0.119

 Mole fraction solubilit1es 1n solvents contain1ng chlorine and boron, wh1ch were
 1nvestigated, are appreciably lower. Values corresponding to 293.15 K are as
 follows :

      butoxyd1chloroborane                          0.0213
      d1chlorophenylborane                          0.0451 (extrapolated)

 Mole fract10n solubilities in boron trichloride, at a partial pressure of
 hydrogen chlor1de of 101.3 kPa, fall below the reference 11ne in the temperature
 range of 208.15 K to 263.15 K. Measurements have not been made outs1de th1s
 range.

CRITICAL EVALUATIO~:

       The Solubility of Hydrogen Chloride          ~n   Solvents Contain~ng Phosphorus.
 Solubil~t~es ~n a variety of solvents contain~ng phosphorus have been
 measured by Gerrard and his co-workers (1-4) over temperature ranges at
 barometric pressure. Data are self-consistent but, only in the case of
 tributyl phosphate can comparison be made with measurements by other
 workers. Bor~ssov & Ionin (5) have published a small diagram showing a
 plot of the logar~thm of the mole ratio solubil~ty at 298.15 K and 101.3
 kPa in f~ve trialkyl esters against the carbon number of the alkyl group.
 In the case of tr~butyl ester the corresponding mole fraction solubil~ty is
 about 0.6 which may be compared with a value of 0.684 by extrapolation of
 measurements by Gerrard et a1.

CRITICAL EVALUATION:

       The Solubility of Hydrogen Chloride in Solvents Contain1ng Silicon.

Gerrard et a1.(1) measured solubilities in four tetraalkyl esters of
sil1cic acid over temperature ranges at a total pressure equal to
101.3 kPa. Solubility over a pressure and temperature range 1n one of
these esters, the tetra(4-methyl-2-pentyl) ester, was reported by these
authors in a later publ1cation (2). Solubilities are very h1gh under the
conditions of measurement. The later measurements show that, at a total
pressure of 101.3 kPa, mole fract10n solub111t1es are not very sensitive to
changes in pressure (see fig. 1). It follows that mole fraction
solub111t1es at a total pressure of 101.3 kPa may be equated with mole
fraction solub1lit1es at a partial pressure of 101.3 kPa for the purpose of
comparison of data w1th those for different systems.
Mole fraction solubil1ties at a total pressure of 101.3 kPa in the
tetraethyl, tetrapropyl and tetra(4-methyl-2-pentyl) esters are close to
each other over the temperature ranges in wh1ch compar1son can be made.
Mole fraction solubilit1es in the tetramethyl ester are close to those in
the tetra(4-methyl-2-pentyl) ester at temperatures less than about 240 K.
Solub111ties 1n all four esters show a marked decrease with 1ncrease 1n
temperature at temperatures above about 283.15 K but this decrease is
especially marked in the case of the tetramethyl ester (see fig. 2).

Gerrard et a1.(2) also measured solubilities 1n the tetrak1s(2-chloro-
ethyl) ester. Mole fraction solubil1t1es at a total pressure of 101.3 kPa
are aga1n higher compared w1th the reference line based upon the Raoult's
law equation but the presence of chlorine reduces solub111ty relat1ve to
the tetraethyl ester (see fig. 2).

Measurements of solub111t1es in the esters of s1licic aC1d discussed above
are consistent over wide temperature ranges. The only measurements
available for comparison are those of the solubilities in the tetraethyl
ester at three temperatures by Ditsent and co-workers which were cited by
Gorshkov et a1.(3). They correspond to lower solubilit1es than found by
Gerrard et a1. Details are not available. They should not be considered
to cast serious doubt on the reliability of Gerrard's data.

Data published by Gorshkov et a1.(3) show that the solubility of hydrogen
chloride in triethoxy silane is also very high with a mole fraction
solubility of about 0.6 at 293.15 K. The solubility was, however, found by
an indirect method based upon kinetic measurements because of chemical
reaction of hydrogen chloride with the solvent. This work must be
considered to have only semi-quantitative significance.
Ahmed, Gerrard & Maladkar (4) measured solubilities in tetrachlorosilane
over the temperature range 243.15 K to 293.15 K at a total pressure of
101.3 kPa. Solubilities are very low compared with those reported for
dissolution in alkyl esters of silicic acid. The solvent is apprec1ably
volatile at the higher temperatures of measurement ( 25.5 kPa at 293.15 K)
and will make a significant contribution to the total pressure. The
evaluator has estimated the mole fraction solubility at a partial pressure
of 101.3 kPa from the solubility data at each temperature given by Ahmed
et a1.  Rau (5) has measured solubilit1es in the same solvent over
partial pressure ranges to a maximum of 0.298 kPa in the temperature range
290 K to 410.5 K. Mole fraction solubilities for a partial pressure of
101.3 kPa are inconsistent with solubilities for lower temperatures from
data by Ahmed et a1. Further work on this system is required.

 The objective of this work was to determine the solubility of HCl in
 component 2, Triethoxysilane. A kinetic method was used. The hydrogen
 chloride reacted with the solvent, which was initially 95.9 % triethoxy-
 silane and 4.1 % silicic acid, tetraethyl ester or tetraethoxysilane, to
 form an intermediate chlorosilane· (chlorodiethoxysilane, C H CI0 Si,
                                                             4 I1   2
 [6485-91-2]) ,ethanol [64-17-5], and hydrogen [1333-74-0] .

The conventional method of determination is frustrated by the occurrence
of an irreversible conversion of the triethoxysilane into tetraethoxysilane
and hydrogen, via an intermediate chlorosilane formulated as (C2H50)2SiHCl.
It was stated that the solubility was determined from kinetic curves, and
the known solubility of HCl in ethanol (1) and in tetraethoxysilane (the
citation being given merely as V. E. Ditsent and co-workers).

The solubility of HCl in monochloridiethoxysilane,(C2H50)2SiHCl [6485-91-2),
could not be determined from the kinetic curves; it was assumed to be half
its solubility in triethoxysilane.   It was stated that the data on the
solubility of HCI in tetraethoxysilane for pressures below 760 mmHg (not
recorded, but presumably those attributed to Ditsent, et aZ.) were used
to convert the mole ratio values for 1 atm (Table above) to those for pres-
sures below 1 atm by assuming that the solubility ratio, (n !n )!(n !n ),

below 1 atm. These calculated data were presented as mole fractions, xl'
for triethoxysilane, as shown on the next page.

       The Solubility of Hydrogen Chlor1de 1n Tetrachlorostannane and in
       Titanium Chloride.

Ahmed et 81.(1) have reported the solubi11ty in tetrachlorostannane at a
total pressure of 101.3 kPa over the temperature range 243.15 K to
293.15 K. The data are self-consistent and likely to be more reliable than
the measurements at 273 K and 300 K reported by Howald & W1llard (2) which
correspond to lower solubilities.   The mole fraction solubil1ty at 273 K
from Ahmed's data 1S 0.061 compared w1th 0.050 from Howald & W1llard's
data. The values for 300 K are 0.048 and 0.040 respectively.

Ahmed et 81. also reported solubility in titanium chloride at the same
pressure over a temperature range of 243.15 K to 293.15 K. Measurements
are self consistent and ind1cate mole fraction solubilit1es lower than for
dissolut1on in tetrachlorostannane. The value of the mole fraction
solubility at 273.15 K is 0.051.

Alkanes
Solub~lity in hexane was measured by Fontana & Herold (1) at 278.15 K and
293.15 K over the pressure range 41.4 kPa to 213.7 kPa and by Boedeker &
Lynch (2) at 298.15 K, 308.15 K and 318.15 K over the pressure range
6.7 kPa to 93.3 kPa. Results were expressed as Henry's constants. Mole
fract~on solub~lit~es at a partial pressure of 101.3 kPa from the sets of
data may be fitted to the equation :
                       -44.591     +   2912.4/(T/K)    +   5.5481 In(T/K)
Th~s equation ~s based upon data for the temperature range 278.15 K to
318.15 K. Extrapolation outs~de this range may lead to error. The standard
deviation in values of x HBr is 0.00089.
Solubility ~n decane at a total pressure of 101.3 kPa over the temperature
range 243.15 K to 293.15 K has been measured by Ahmed et a1.(3) and at
298.15 K to 319.15 K in the pressure range 6.7 kPa to 92.3 kPa by Boedeker
& Lynch (2). The latter reported Henry's constants for three temperatures
rather than measurements of solub~l~ty at ~nd~vidual pressures. Mole
fraction solub~l~tles at a partial pressure of 101.3 kPa from these Henry's
constants show good cons~stency with values for lower temperature from
Ahmed's data. The mole fraction solubility at 101.3 kPa by extrapolat~on
of values based upon Ahmed's data ~s 0.0497 compared with the value of
0.0519 from the Henry's constant at this temperature published by Boedeker
& Lynch. Mole fract~on solublllt~es at 101.3 kPa from the two sources may
be f~tted to the equation :

                       -73.774    +    4380.1/(T/K)    +   9.8532 In(T/K)
The standard deviation in values of x HBr         ~s   0.0020.

Solubility in butane at 278.15 K and 298.15 K over a pressure range from
41.4 kPa to 213.7 kPa was measured by Fontana & Herold (1). Solubil~ty in
octane at partial pressures from 0.067 to 93.3 kPa at 298.15 K, 308.15 K
and 318.15 K was measured by Boedeker & Lynch (2). In each case data were
reported as Henry's constants from which mole fraction solubil~ties at a
partial pressure of 101.3 kPa may be calculated.

Solubility in heptane at a total pressure of 101.3 kPa over a temperature
range from 233.15 K to 293.15 K was measured by Ahmed et a1.(3).

Mole fraction solubilities at 298.15 K for a partial pressure of hydrogen
bromide of 101.3 kPa, on the basis of the available data, are as follows:

 butane    0.0332

CRITICAL EVALUATIO:-';

 The available data for solubilities of hydrogen bromide in butane, heptane
 and octane are conS1stent with measurements of the solubilities of this gas
 1n hexane and in decane which have been studied by more than one group.
 Solubi11ties in these three solvents may be accepted on a tentat1ve bas1s.

 Fontana & Herold (1) also showed that the mole fraction solub1lity in
 butane and in hexane are reduced in the presence of aluminium bromide under
 the conditions of their measurements. The accuracy of these additional
 measurements cannot be evaluated.
 Aromatic hydrocarbons

 Mole fraction solubilities in aromatic hydrocarbons at a part1al pressure
 of gas of 101.3 kPa over the temperature range in which measurements are
 ava1lable l1e above the reference line based upon the Raoult's law equat10n
 and increase 1n the order:
   benzene < methylbenzene < 1,3-dimethylbenzene < 1,3,5-trimethylbenzene
 Solubility in benzene in the range 263.15 K to 293.15 K at a total pressure
 of 101.3 kPa was measured by Ahmed et 81.(3). O'Brien & Bobalek (4)
 reported solub1lity at 298.15 K over the partial pressure range 0.111 kPa
 to 57.2 kPa, Kapustinskii & Mal'tsev (5) at 303.15 K & 323.15 K over the
 range 1.02 kPa to 84.35 kPa and Brown & Wallace (6) at 278.85 K at
 pressures to 20 kPa. Ahmed's data have been corrected to give values of
 the mole fraction solubi11ty at a partial pressure of 101.3 kPa. Other
 data have been extrapolated to this pressure. The smoothing equation for
 mole fraction solubi11ty at a partial pressure of 101.3 kPa based upon the
 data available for the temperature range 263.15 K to 323.15 K is :

                          115.68      3357.2/(T/K)           18.780 In(T/K)

 Values of x    fit this equation with a standard deviation of 0.0054.
            HBr
 Ahmed et 81.(3) have also reported the solub1l1ty in methylbenzene at a
 total pressure of 101.3 kPa in the temperature range 233.15 K to 293.15 K.
 O'Br1en & Bobalek (4) measured the solubility at 298.15 K over a partial
 pressure range of 19.47 kPa to 47.73 kPa and Brown & Wallace (6) at
 273.15 K and pressures to 18.7 kPa. Mole fraction solubilities by
 extrapolation or by correction to a partial pressure of 101.3 kPa may be
 fitted to the equation :

                         71.850     1427.6/(T/K)        12.212 In(T/K)

 Values of x HBr fit this equation with a standard deviation of 0.0091.
 Ahmed et 81.(3) measured the solubility in 1 ,3-dimethylbenzene at a total
 pressure of 101.3 kPa over the temperature range 233.15 K to 293.15 K. The
 difference between these measurements and the solubility at a part1al
 pressure of gas of 101.3 kPa is likely to be less than experimental error.
 The mole fraction solubility for a partial pressure of 101.3 kPa at
 273.15 K based upon these measurements is 0.134. This differs from the
 value of 0.204 corresponding to the Henry's constant from measurements to
 15.3 kPa reported by Brown & Wallace (6) and based upon the assumption that
 the variation of mole fraction solubility with pressure is linear to 101.3
 kPa.   If the variation approximates to that expressed by the Margules
 equation then the mole fraction solubility at 101.325 kPa, corresponding
 to Brown & Wallace's measurement, would be about 0.16. This is closer to
 Ahmed's value.

 Ahmed's data are likely to give a better measure of the solubility at a
 partial pressure of 101.3 kPa. They should be treated as tentative values
 until further measurements on the system are available.

Brown & Wallace (6) also measured the solubility in 1,3,5-trimethylbenzene
at 273.15 K to 14.67 kPa. Measurements indicate that, to this pressure at
least, solub~lity ~s greater than in 1 ,3-d~methylbenzene. Linear
extrapolation to a part~al pressure of 101.3 kPa gives a value of the mole
fraction solubil~ty of 0.226. If, however, the var~ation of mole fraction
solubility w~th change of partial pressure approximates to the Margules
equation then the mole fraction solubility at a partial pressure of
101.3 kPa would be about 0.17. These extrapolated values should be
considered to be of semi-quantitat~ve s~gnificance only.

Alkanols
Mole fraction solubilities in alkanols at a partial pressure of 101.3 kPa
are appreciably higher than values represented by a reference line based
upon the Raoult's law equation applied to hydrogen bromide. Mole fraction
solub~lities of hydrogen chloride show similar h~gh values relat~ve to the
correspond~ng reference line for hydrogen chloride.


The mole fraction solubility ~n ethanol from data reported by Dorofeeva (7)
is 0.285 at 298.15 K. It is not clear whether th~s corresponds to a total
or to a part~al pressure of 101.325 kPa as no details of the measurements

Solubility in 1-octanol at a total pressure of 101.3 kPa was measured by

part~al pressure of the solvent makes insign~f~cant contribution to the

of 101.3 kPa in the range 288.15 K to 333.15 was measured by Fernandes (8).
There is good agreement between solubilities over the few degrees in wh~ch
the measurements overlap. At 288.15 K the interpolated value of mole
fraction solub~lity from Ahmed's data is 0.530. The value given by
Fernandes is 0.519. However the slopes of the curves of mole fract~on
solubillty against temperature differ in the two cases so that extrapolated
data from one source are not compatible with data from the other source.
(fig. 1)

       ln x    = 31.5861   - 892.58/(T/K) - 5.1505 In(T/K)

The standard deviation in values of x HBr is 0.021.

cons~dered to be tentative. It should not be used to estimate solubilities

Substitution of chlorine 1nto an alcohol lowers the solubility of hydrogen
chloride in that alcohol. The solub1lity of hydrogen bromide 1n
2-chloroethanol, 2,2-dichloroethanol and in 2,2,2-tr1chloroethanol have
been reported by Gerrard & co-workers for a pressure of 101.3 kPa within

solub1l1ty in 2,2,2-trichloroethanol are conta1ned in two papers from the

higher end of the temperature ranges. Mole fraction solub1lities at
273.15 K, 283.15 K and 293.15 K from the earlier paper (10) are
respect1vely 0.161, 0.130 and 0.0944. Values for these temperatures from

The mole fraction solubil1ty of hydrogen bromide in ethanol at 298.15 K and
101.325 kPa, from Dorofeeva's measurements discussed above, does not f1t
into the pattern. This value of 0.285 is less than the correspond1ng value
of 0.377 for dissolution in 2-chloroethanol. The data for the chlorinated
compound are likely to be the more reliable.

              The values of Henry's constant, K/atm, and the mole fraction
              solubility at one atm were calculated by the compiler.

              The data were given simply as Henry's constant, K/mmHg, and as
              a straight line plot of Xl and total pressure (4 points) .

              Henry's constant for an "ideal solution" was taken as the
              vapor pressure of pure liquid HBr (11850 mmHg or 15.59 atm)
              estimated from data reported by Bates, Halford and Anderson (1).
              The value from the International Critiaal Tables (2) is 14.3
              atm.

              The mole fraction solubility was calculated assuming Henry's
              law is obeyed up to a pressure of one atm, thus Xl = l/(K/atm).

                               AUXILIARY INFORMATION
 METHOD/APPARATUS/PROCEDURE:
 Two methods were used:
Weight Increase method.  This method was used when the estimated vapor
pressure of the alcohol was less than one mmHg. A 15-20 g sample of
alcohol was placed in a clean, dry, weighed saturator and weiged. The
saturator and contents were thermostatted. HBr gas was passed through the
liquid for about one hour. The saturator and contents were weighed. The
process was repeated until two successive readings agreed.

Acid-base titratIon method.  The alcohol was saturated with HBr as in the
weight increase method. A 1-2 cm 3 sample of the saturated solut~on was
taken in a clean, dry and weighed sample tube; weighed and transferred to a
flask containing a known amount of chilled standard NaOH solution. After
reaction of the HBr and NaOH the excess base was titrated w~th a standard
HCl solution.
The methods agreed within 1% by weight.
 SOURCE AND PURITY OF MATERIALS:
(1) Hydrogen bromide. Matheson Co., Inc.          Stated to be 99.8% pure.        Used
    as received
(2) Alkanols.    K and K Labs. Reagent grade.            Minimum purity 99%.   Used as
   . received.
ESTIMATED ERROR:
One percent by weight.

     Appendix I summarizes some physical property values of the hydrogen
halides which will be of interest to the users of the solubility data. The
property values are based on data in the IntepnationaZ CpiticaZ TabZes (ref
1), NBS CipcuZap 500(ref 2) ,The Handbook of Chemistpy and Physics, 64th Ed.
(ref 3), and recent measurements of Henderson at aZ. (ref 4) on hydrogen
chloride. The data were evaluated at time of publication, but the user
should be alert for more up to date values in future pUblications. The data
given here are believed to be adequate for most applications related to the
solubility of the hydrogen halides.
     Below are values of the enthalpy, entropy and heat capacity changes on
fusion and on vaporization at atmospheric pressure. The values have been
recalculated in kJ and J from values given in NBS CipcuZap 500. The tempera-
tures for fusion and vaporization from CipcuZap 500 are given in Table I on
the following page.
Substance          f,H/kJ mol- 1           M/J K- 1 mol- 1                    I mol-I
                                                                     f,Cp/J K

              Fusion   Vaporization Fusion        Vaporization Fusion       Vaporization

 HF             4.58         7.5        24.1           25.5          10.7       -46
 HCl            1.99        16.2        12.5           85.8           8.8       -29.9
 HBr            2.41        17.6        12.9           85.3           6.9       -30.8
 HI             2.87        19.8        12.9           83.1           4.6       -29.9

The enthalpy change on vaporization of HCl is 16.194 kJ mol-I at the normal
boiling point according to Henderson et aZ. (ref 4) .
     Table I gives the fusion and normal boiling point temperatures, the
critical temperatures and pressures, and the ideal mole fraction solubility
at a number of temperatures at a gas partial pressure of one atmosphere.
     The fusion and normal boiling point temperatures of HF, HBr and HI
were taken from CipcuZap 500, the values of HCl are from Henderson et aZ.
The critical property values were taken from the compilation of R. Loebel
in the Handbook of Chemistpy and Physics. The critical temperature and
pressure of HCl are from Henderson et aZ. The critical values differ by
only about one percent from values given in the IntepnationaZ CpiticaZ
TabZes which were compiled from data taken before 1928.
     The ideal mole fraction solubilities are based on Raoults law. The
values are for a gas partial pressure of one atm. For HF the required
vapor pressures were calculated from the equation given in the Handbook of
Chemistpy and Physics. For HCl, HBr and HI the vapor pressures were taken
from the IntepnationaZ CpiticaZ TabZes. The ideal mole fraction solubility
values are useful in discussions about the departure of solubility from
ideal behavior and the Gerrard Reference Line.
